title: Locks, shared memory and concurrency
one_liner: Postgres backends share one memory region and use four kinds of locks, from tiny spinlocks to deadlock-checked table locks, to avoid stepping on each other.
analogy: A busy kitchen: one shared pantry (shared memory), a quick hand-grab rule (spinlock), a queue for the recipe book (LWLock), and a booking sheet for tables (heavyweight locks).
big_picture: The postmaster creates one big shared memory block at startup. Every backend inherits it through fork().
In the normal fork build, the main segment is inherited at the same address, so plain pointers work. Dynamic shared memory (DSM) segments are not, so they use relative pointers.
Spinlocks are the smallest lock. They busy-wait and protect only a few instructions.
LWLocks guard shared data structures. They have shared and exclusive modes and sleep when blocked.
Heavyweight locks guard user-visible things like tables and rows. They have 8 modes and deadlock detection.
Latches wake sleeping processes. Wait events tell pg_stat_activity what a backend is waiting for.

flow.step: Postmaster sizes and builds shared memory
flow.detail: CalculateShmemSize adds up every subsystem. CreateSharedMemoryAndSemaphores then makes the one big segment.
Each subsystem lists a request_fn and init_fn (ShmemCallbacks). It calls ShmemRequestStruct to name and size its area.

flow.step: Backend starts and joins the ProcArray
flow.detail: Each backend owns a PGPROC slot. ProcArrayAdd puts it in the list that snapshots scan.

flow.step: Query asks for a table lock
flow.detail: LockAcquireExtended tries the fast path for weak locks. If that is not allowed it uses the shared lock hash table.
JoinWaitQueue puts the backend on the lock wait queue. ProcSleep then starts the deadlock_timeout timer and sleeps on a latch.
CheckDeadLock calls DeadLockCheck, which looks for cycles in the wait graph. It may reorder the queue or raise an error.
LockRelease or LockReleaseAll frees the lock. ProcWakeup grants it to waiters and sets their latch.
CommitTransaction calls ProcArrayEndTransaction to clear the xid, then releases locks via ResourceOwnerRelease.
flow.where: src/backend/access/transam/xact.c: CommitTransaction; src/backend/utils/resowner/resowner.c: ResourceOwnerRelease; proc.c: ProcReleaseLocks

diagram.claim: A backend takes a table lock, may wait on a latch, and is woken by the lock holder; the deadlock check runs on a timer.

interview.q: Why does Postgres use shared memory, and who creates it?
answer: Backends are separate processes. They need one place to share locks, buffers and the ProcArray.
The postmaster creates it once at startup. Children inherit it via fork().
In the fork build the main segment has the same address in all processes, so plain pointers work. DSM segments do not, so they use relative pointers.
Allocated memory is never freed. Hash tables reuse entries through free lists.
interview.trap: Shared memory is not resizable at runtime. Changing size needs a restart.

interview.q: What are the four kinds of locks in Postgres?
answer: Spinlocks: tiny, busy-wait, no deadlock detection.
LWLocks: shared or exclusive, guard shared structures, released automatically on error.
Regular (heavyweight) locks: table-driven modes, deadlock detection, released at transaction end.
SIReadLock predicate locks: used by SERIALIZABLE, they never block anyone.
interview.trap: Predicate locks do not block. They only record read dependencies.

interview.q: When should you use a spinlock instead of an LWLock?
answer: Only for a few instructions with no function calls that can block and no kernel calls.
Waiters spin and retry with growing sleeps. After NUM_DELAYS (1000) tries, s_lock_stuck reports an error.
If you need to hold it longer or read shared state for a while, use an LWLock.
interview.trap: Do not hold a spinlock across a palloc, elog or I/O call.

interview.q: How does an LWLock work and what happens when it is contended?
answer: One atomic state word holds the shared-holder count, an exclusive bit and a has-waiters flag (LW_FLAG_HAS_WAITERS).
If the lock is free, LWLockAcquire just does an atomic update. This is fast.
If not, LWLockQueueSelf adds the backend to a wait list and it sleeps on its semaphore.
Waiters wake roughly in order. A run of shared waiters wakes together, an exclusive waiter wakes alone. LWLockReleaseAll runs on error recovery.
interview.trap: LWLocks have no deadlock detection and no timeout. Lock ordering is your job.

interview.q: What are the heavyweight lock modes and how is a conflict decided?
answer: Eight modes, from AccessShareLock (SELECT) to AccessExclusiveLock (ALTER TABLE, DROP TABLE).
Each LOCK has a grantMask bitmask of held modes.
A request conflicts if its row in the conflict table ANDed with grantMask is non-zero (LockCheckConflicts).
Readers (AccessShare) do not conflict with writers (RowExclusive).
interview.trap: SELECT still takes a table lock. It is just a weak one that rarely conflicts.

interview.q: What is the fast-path lock and why does it exist?
answer: Most queries take weak locks on tables that nobody else locks strongly.
Fast path stores them in the backend's own PGPROC slots, guarded by a per-backend LWLock.
This avoids the busy shared lock hash table partitions.
A strong lock (like AccessExclusive) first bumps FastPathStrongRelationLocks, then moves other backends' fast-path locks into the main table.
interview.trap: Fast path is only for weak locks on non-shared relations. It is not used for every lock.

interview.q: How does Postgres detect a deadlock?
answer: A backend waits first. After deadlock_timeout (default 1s) a timer calls CheckDeadLock in proc.c.
DeadLockCheck builds a wait-for graph and searches for a cycle.
Hard edges cannot be changed. Soft edges (queue order) can be reordered to avoid the cycle.
If no reorder helps, the backend that found the cycle errors out.
interview.trap: Detection does not run on every wait. That would be expensive.

interview.q: How do latches and wait events fit in?
answer: A latch is a flag a process can sleep on. SetLatch wakes it and WaitLatch waits.
Pattern: ResetLatch, check the condition, then WaitLatch. This avoids lost wakeups.
Before sleeping, code calls pgstat_report_wait_start with an ID from wait_event_names.txt.
That ID shows up as wait_event in pg_stat_activity.
interview.trap: Check the condition between ResetLatch and WaitLatch. Otherwise you can miss a wakeup.

interview.q: How do row locks differ from table locks, and what is SSI?
answer: Row locks live in the tuple header (xmax), not the lock table. See README.tuplock and heap_lock_tuple in heapam.c.
Waiting on a row actually waits on the other transaction's ID via XactLockTableWait.
Under SERIALIZABLE, SSI records reads as SIReadLocks (predicate.c) and tracks rw-conflicts.
A dangerous structure of two adjacent rw-conflict edges causes a serialization failure.
interview.trap: Row locks do not fill up the shared lock table, so locking millions of rows is fine.

contributor_tips: Read src/backend/storage/lmgr/README first, then skim lock.c along its function list.
Add a test or doc fix around wait events in src/backend/utils/activity/wait_event_names.txt as a gentle first patch.
Always keep spinlock sections tiny and never call anything that can error while holding one.
Use pg_locks and pg_stat_activity on a running server to see the code you read.
